subject: Archaeology
title: The Antikythera Mechanism
description: A 60-second lesson on The Antikythera Mechanism.

hook.text: In 1901, divers found a corroded lump of bronze in a Greek shipwreck. It sat in a museum for decades.

buildup.text: X-ray imaging in the 1970s revealed dozens of interlocking gears inside — a 2,100-year-old computer.

discovery.text: The device predicted eclipses, tracked planetary positions, and even timed the ancient Olympic Games.

twist.text: Nothing this complex appeared again in Europe for over 1,000 years. The technology was completely lost.

climax.text: Modern engineers needed advanced tools to build a working replica. Ancient Greeks did it by hand.

punchline.text: The Greeks built a computer 2,000 years before the Industrial Revolution.

quiz.question: What did the Antikythera Mechanism do?
options: It was a navigational tool for ancient sailors
It predicted eclipses, tracked planets, and timed the Olympic Games
It calculated taxes for the Greek government

details.summary: The Antikythera Mechanism, recovered from a 1st-century BCE shipwreck in 1901, is the world's oldest known analog computer. Its complex system of bronze gears predicted astronomical events with remarkable precision, representing technology unseen again for over a thousand years.
details.whyItMatters: This single artifact fundamentally changed historians' assessment of ancient Greek technological capability. It proves that ancient civilizations achieved mechanical sophistication that was lost and not replicated until the medieval period.
takeaways: Recovered from a Greek shipwreck in 1901
Contains at least 30 interlocking bronze gears
Predicted eclipses and planetary positions with precision

faq.question: How complex is the Antikythera Mechanism?
faq.answer: It contains at least 30 bronze gears with precisely cut teeth, encoding astronomical cycles including the Metonic cycle, Saros eclipse cycle, and the irregular orbit of the Moon. Modern researchers needed X-ray tomography and decades of study to understand its full capabilities.

faq.question: Why was this technology lost?
faq.answer: The knowledge required to build such devices was likely held by a small community of specialists. Roman conquest disrupted Greek scientific traditions. Without institutional transmission of knowledge, the expertise died with its practitioners and mechanical complexity regressed for centuries.
